F-003.reason: At HEAD, run_connection sends Ack{seq} right after apply(), and the inbox is memory-only, so a daemon restart loses messages that were applied but not delivered. That breaks C-029/C-043. An uncommitted fix (ack_point) is in progress in the working tree, but it is not committed. It also leaves a gap: after a restart, the replayed broadcast and user messages fan out to self.sessions.keys(), which is empty until sessions say hello again, so those messages still reach nobody.

F-004.reason: At HEAD, apply() drops every seq <= last_seq, and the daemon ignores the head sent in Welcome. A hub database reset, or a WAL commit lost on power failure under synchronous=NORMAL (which really is non-durable on power loss), therefore makes the daemon silently drop new events. An uncommitted fix that resets last_seq to the head is in the working tree. Residual risk: if the hub has already grown past the daemon's old cursor before it reconnects, the reused seqs in between are still dropped.

F-005.reason: The code matches the finding: host is lowercased, path case is kept, and ssh host aliases are not resolved. But the common forms that matter do agree: git@github.com:owner/repo and https://github.com/owner/repo both normalise to github.com/owner/repo. The trap bites only checkouts that use differently-cased paths or custom ssh aliases. It would be settled by checking the remotes the team actually uses. Either way, the brief should state the limit instead of 'shared across checkouts'.

F-006.reason: Three of the four sub-claims hold in the code. (1) In pre_tool_use, a renew rejected for a stale token is followed by a fresh acquire, and on a grant the 'lost' flag is never shown, so the session is not told it lost the lease, which defeats the fencing promise in C-031. (2) The hub emits lease.expired, but state.rs has no handler for it, so expiry is silent. (3) In transfer(), the conflict check counts the grantor's own sub-lease. The area: sub-claim is by design: areas are advertised as named, advisory scopes. The bare-directory point stands, though: scope() accepts 'src' or 'src/' without complaint and it overlaps no file.

Protected paths are also enforced only for edit tools, and only when the hub answers. The brief contradicts itself: C-044 describes a working-tree watcher and a pre-commit check, while C-059 says they are not built. Calling 'protected' paths a deny is an overclaim at the trust level the brief states.

F-009.reason: The brief's own security scope (C-064) includes local endpoint misuse, and the bearer token only makes sense if other local principals exist. A squatter on 127.0.0.1:7421 while the daemon is down gets more than the token: it receives every hook body, including UserPromptSubmit prompts and edit tool_input. A settings.local.json written with the default umask is readable by other members of the staff group under a default macOS home directory. Severity is moderate on single-user machines.

F-010.reason: The code already does what the underlying problem asks for. A PREAMBLE says relayed blocks are information, not instructions. The permission relay is never declared, which matches C-039 and the channels-reference L496 advice. Hooks never return allow, so the user's permission prompts stay in force. Malicious trusted peers are out of scope (C-065). What remains is the wording in C-038: 'cannot pass as the user's instruction' promises more than wrapping can guarantee against a peer agent that has itself been injected. It would be settled by rewording C-038 as a mitigation, not a guarantee.

F-011.reason: The brief already discloses the duplicate (C-054), every block already carries a seq attribute (from_attrs), and the duplicate happens only when channels are enabled. Relayed text is framed as information, so a duplicate usually costs nothing. What is missing is only one line in the preamble telling the model to act once per seq. It would be settled by a real session that receives a duplicated request and either repeats the action or does not.

F-012.reason: The brief already lists no rate limits and no event pruning as known gaps (C-059, C-062), and puts trusted-peer DoS out of scope (C-065). Each session is bounded at 100 inbox notices and 8,000 characters of context, and idle-session wake (asyncRewake) is unverified, so an agent-to-agent loop moves forward only while both sessions are active. That makes this a storage and token-cost bound, not a runaway. It would be settled by a two-session auto-reply test that measures growth.

F-014.reason: The code matches the finding: hub.replay() is awaited before the select loop and inside the Lagged arm, so requests wait while the hub replays. The only effect is fail-open: lease checks pass their 800 ms deadline and return a stale notice. Replay is capped at 100,000 events in batches of 500, and on localhost it takes milliseconds. It would be settled by timing a worst-case replay over a real tailnet.

F-015.reason: Real but conditional. who_text lists up to 30 sessions from every repo before this repo's leases, and block() cuts the body at MAX_BLOCK, 2,000 characters. At roughly 100-150 characters per session line, leases fall off only past about 12-15 other sessions, which is unlikely for a small trusted tailnet. It would be settled by the expected session count. Listing this repo's leases first is still a cheap fix.

An unpinned stable toolchain and the first-party actions/checkout@v4 tag are hygiene issues, not an unpinned-dependency trap. Optional polish: add --locked to the README.
